summary: This memo describes how to carry SNMP over AppleTalk instead of UDP and IP, so network management can work on AppleTalk networks. It is historic.

eli5.summary: SNMP is how network managers ask devices questions. This paper shows how to send the same questions over AppleTalk, the networking system used by Apple computers back then. It is historic.

questions: how to run snmp on appletalk networks
how does snmp run on appletalk networks
why did snmp over appletalk fade
subtitle: Run SNMP network management on AppleTalk instead of UDP and IP.

tldr.problem: Many AppleTalk-only network devices in the 1990s lacked TCP/IP support but needed to be monitored and managed. SNMP was the standard for network management, but it was designed for TCP/IP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to encapsulate SNMP messages inside AppleTalk's Datagram Delivery Protocol (DDP) instead of UDP, allowing SNMP to manage AppleTalk devices using AppleTalk's Name Binding Protocol for discovery.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is historic. As TCP/IP became universal and AppleTalk networks faded, the need for SNMP over AppleTalk evaporated. TCP/IP remains the preferred transport for SNMP when available.

today: RFC 1419 is Historic. AppleTalk networks largely disappeared as TCP/IP became universal. Any AppleTalk devices still in operation today would typically also have TCP/IP support, making UDP/IP the preferred transport for SNMP.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) was designed to run over UDP/IP. This RFC extends SNMP to work over AppleTalk, enabling management of network devices that support AppleTalk but lack TCP/IP.

Many non-Internet devices during the 1990s were equipped with AppleTalk protocols. Running SNMP over AppleTalk allowed administrators to monitor and manage these devices using the same SNMP tools and framework they used elsewhere, without requiring them to add TCP/IP support.

The specification is straightforward: SNMP messages are carried inside AppleTalk's DDP (Datagram Delivery Protocol) layer, and device discovery uses AppleTalk's Name Binding Protocol (NBP).
sections.eli5: Think of SNMP like a telegram service. Normally it travels on TCP/IP roads. This document says you can also send it on AppleTalk roads, letting you manage Apple computers that only speak AppleTalk.

sections.title: AppleTalk Basics
sections.content:
DDP (Datagram Delivery Protocol): AppleTalk's connectionless transport layer, equivalent to UDP in TCP/IP. DDP datagrams can carry 0 to 586 octets of data and include source and destination network numbers, node numbers, socket numbers, and a protocol type field.

NBP (Name Binding Protocol): AppleTalk's distributed name-to-address mapping service. An NBP name has the form object:type@zone, where object is a unique name, type categorizes the service, and zone identifies the network segment. Each field is limited to 32 octets and is not case-sensitive.

Unlike TCP/IP where addresses are stable IP numbers, AppleTalk network addresses can change on reboot. Therefore, SNMP over AppleTalk relies on stable NBP names rather than addresses for identifying devices.
sections.eli5: AppleTalk has DDP, which is like UDP for sending short messages. It also has NBP, which is like a name directory that you can look up—"find the printer named LaserWriter in the office zone."

sections.title: SNMP Message Encapsulation
sections.content:
SNMP Requests: Sent to DDP socket 8 with protocol type 8. The DDP datagram's data portion contains a standard SNMP message.

SNMP Responses: Sent back to the originating DDP socket (not necessarily socket 8) with protocol type 8. The source address of the response is the destination address of the request.

SNMP Traps: Sent to DDP socket 9 with protocol type 8. The agent-addr field is filled with all zeros (the unknown IP address in AppleTalk context). To identify the trap sender, the agent must include its NBP name in the variable-bindings.

Agent advertisement: Devices respond to SNMP requests via AppleTalk must advertise using NBP type SNMP Agent. Management stations receiving traps must advertise using NBP type SNMP Trap Handler. These NBP names should be stable and stored in persistent storage.
sections.eli5: SNMP questions go to socket 8. Answers come back to wherever the question came from. Alerts (traps) go to socket 9. Each device registers its name in the NBP directory so managers can find it.

sections.title: Addressing and Name Resolution Strategy
sections.content:
AppleTalk's dynamic address assignment (addresses can change on reboot) creates challenges for management stations. Unlike TCP/IP systems with stable IP addresses, AppleTalk systems are identified by their NBP names.

Caching names: Management stations should cache NBP name-to-address mappings and reuse them for multiple requests. Caches should persist across reboots to reduce network traffic.

Cache lifetime: A cached mapping should be reconfirmed if it is older than T1 seconds (minimum 60 seconds, configurable). A management station can use an NBP confirm (unicast to the cached address) to check if a mapping is still valid.

Implicit confirmation: A management station can confirm a mapping using SNMP itself: include a request for the device's NBP name in the same SNMP packet. If the response includes matching name information, the address is confirmed.

When NBP breaks: If NBP name lookups fail but direct communication is possible, a management station can send NBP forwarding requests to routers or attempt network-wide broadcasts. The specification suggests dedicated management stations might implement router-level NBP functions.
sections.eli5: Since AppleTalk addresses are temporary, managers look up names once and remember them. If an answer gets stale, they ask the device again to confirm the address is still correct. If NBP stops working, clever managers can send the question directly to known networks.

sections.title: Security and Race Conditions
sections.content:
The specification notes a race condition in set-requests: if an old node goes down and a new node comes up with the same DDP address before the cache entry expires, a set-request might go to the wrong agent. The wrong agent could send a response indistinguishable from the intended agent.

This problem is inherent to using addresses instead of authenticated identities. The RFC suggests that future SNMP security mechanisms (with authentication) would prevent this, as the reply would be authenticated to the intended agent.

Agents should be configured with explicit addresses of management stations before sending traps; they must not perform wildcard NBP lookups for trap recipients. In contrast, a management station can do broader lookups to discover agents.
sections.eli5: There is a small risk: if a device breaks and another takes over its address before the manager's cache expires, the manager might talk to the wrong device. Future security will fix this by verifying who is answering.

sections.title: Related SNMP Over Protocol RFCs
sections.content:
This RFC is part of a family of specifications describing how to run SNMP over various non-UDP transports:

  • RFC 1089 (SNMP over Ethernet): SNMP directly over Ethernet, for devices without TCP/IP
  • RFC 1420 (SNMP over IPX): SNMP over Novell's Internetwork Packet Exchange, for managing NetWare devices

All share the same principle: define a mapping from the standard SNMP PDU to the target protocol's datagram format, define a discovery mechanism using that protocol's naming service, and handle the protocol-specific addressing quirks.
sections.eli5: Three networks (Ethernet, AppleTalk, IPX) all needed SNMP. Each RFC specifies how to send the same SNMP messages over that network's native protocol.
